content: Pain experienced during childbirth is often considered one of the most intense forms of pain that some women may encounter in their lifetime. Epidural analgesia is a highly effective method for managing pain during labor. However, many women express concerns about its safety. Additionally, the availability of epidural services and anesthetic support is not consistent across all healthcare facilities. Observational studies have suggested that initiating epidural analgesia early in labor may increase the likelihood of cesarean delivery. However, this association has not been confirmed in more recent randomized controlled trials. Current guidelines indicate that, in the absence of medical contraindications, a maternal request for pain relief is a sufficient medical justification for providing epidural analgesia. The choice of analgesic technique, medication, and dosage depends on several factors, including the patient’s preferences, medical condition, and any contraindications. Despite this, there has been no systematic review of the maternal and fetal outcomes or the safety of early versus late initiation of epidural analgesia. The objective of this systematic review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of early initiation compared to late initiation of epidural analgesia during labor. The review focused on obstetric and fetal outcomes relevant to women, as well as potential side effects of the treatments, including the risk of cesarean delivery, instrumental delivery, and the duration of labor. To gather data, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, and reference lists of relevant studies. The search covered studies published up to February 2014. Only randomized controlled trials comparing early versus late initiation of epidural analgesia in laboring women were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of the studies, extracted data, and evaluated the quality of the trials. The accuracy of the data was verified. The review included nine studies involving a total of 15,752 women. The overall risk of bias in the studies was low, except for performance bias due to the lack of blinding of participants and personnel. The findings revealed no clinically significant difference in the risk of cesarean delivery between early and late initiation of epidural analgesia (risk ratio [RR] 1.02; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.96 to 1.08; nine studies, 15,499 women; high-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no clinically significant difference in the risk of instrumental delivery (RR 0.93; 95% CI 0.86 to 1.01; eight studies, 15,379 women; high-quality evidence). The duration of the second stage of labor did not differ significantly between early and late initiation of epidural analgesia (mean difference [MD] -3.22 minutes; 95% CI -6.71 to 0.27; eight studies, 14,982 women; high-quality evidence). However, there was significant variability in the duration of the first stage of labor, and the data could not be pooled for analysis. There was no clinically significant difference in Apgar scores of less than seven at one minute (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.10; seven studies, 14,924 women; high-quality evidence) or at five minutes (RR 0.96; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.33; seven studies, 14,924 women; high-quality evidence). Additionally, there was no meaningful difference in umbilical arterial pH between early and late initiation of epidural analgesia (MD 0.01; 95% CI -0.01 to 0.03; four studies, 14,004 women; high-quality evidence). Similarly, no significant difference was observed in umbilical venous pH, although the evidence quality was moderate (MD 0.01; 95% CI -0.00 to 0.02; four studies, 14,004 women). The authors concluded that high-quality evidence suggests that early and late initiation of epidural analgesia during labor have comparable effects on all measured outcomes. However, it is important to note that women allocated to delayed epidural groups often received alternative forms of pain relief during the waiting period, which complicates the interpretation of the outcomes. For first-time mothers in labor who request epidural analgesia for pain relief, the timing of epidural initiation should primarily depend on the woman’s preference.
